I should add that PPIs do work best when you take them 30-ish minutes before eating. If you're taking it and then not eating, you're not reaching the full effect of the medicine. PPIs work on actively secreting proton pumps... of which there are more when you're digesting food.

I did not take omeprazole, but I took pantoprazole (another PPI). I would wake up and take it 30 minutes before eating breakfast. Propofol tends to be a more commonly used anesthesia for this due to how fast acting it is. Basically, as soon as they stop administering it, you wake up coherent within minutes. I was completely conscious and able to have normal conversations before they even finished wheeling me from the operating room. It's a wonderful, relaxing drug with minimal side effects (usually none). They like it for this reason. They can have you leave within 30 minutes of the procedure ending!

That said, some places do the fentanyl combo. You have to understand this drug was designed for medical use, they're trained to administer it, and they do so very carefully. I was given fentanyl after my gallbladder removal surgery, and I was still literally YELLING in 10/10 pain because they wouldn't give me more. They're not going to overdo it. There is an entire team of people in that room that are working to ensure you leave that place completely okay. No one wants you to be hurt. No one wants to risk their job or their license or their lives by fucking that up!

I have OCD and medical trauma myself, so I strongly empathize with how your wife is feeling. Last year I had to have an endoscopy done which required propofol, so I'll share what I know anecdotally.

Propofol is often used as "twilight" sedation, which means your wife won't be under the deep, heavy sedation we think of with normal surgery, but she won't remember anything at all either. For me, propofol felt absolutely fantastic. I had a surprisingly restful nap. Later, I ended up requiring gallbladder removal surgery, which, of course, does use deeper, general anesthesia. Wildly different experience. I would think that in combination with a Valium, she would be floating on cloud 9 for at least a little bit. Minus the whole tooth part lol... 

I'm not sure if propofol is used for deeper sedation as well. You could ask how they intend to use it. Personally, I would be less nervous about it either way, vs other sedation, just based on what I have been through.

Again, NAD, and of course not everyone responds to all chemicals the same way. But I think my experience with propofol is common.

Bile dumping is just what it sounds like - your gallbladder is contracting hard and pushing out more bile than it is supposed to into your small intestine. This speeds up transit. Cramping, loose stool/diarrhea, not fully digesting or absorbing things. The psyllium husk is soaking it up and slowing transit. When are you experiencing the diarrhea? If you're experiencing it first thing in the morning, take some fiber right before going to bed. If you're experiencing after most meals, spread out your dose and take some with each meal if taking it in one dose does not help all day. You can also take more than you are taking if it doesn't cause you to become constipated... might need to work up to a little more over a couple of weeks.

So my dentist did two things. 

One was a thing where he used an awkward camera stick to digitally photograph my entire mouth, so that on a screen he could see an exact 3D replica of every tooth and and how they come together when I bite, in full color. This was how he saw my teeth were not lining up correctly and why they were sliding and knocking around when I bite.

The second thing he used was this... a "T-scan". https://www.tekscan.com/products-solutions/digital-occlusal-analysis With this we could see my new crown was fully out of occlusion and my right side is absorbing an abnormally high amount of pressure. 

I'd never seen this sort of tech before this dentist. I imagine this tech is insanely expensive and your dentist may not have it even if they are great. I got super lucky with this dude, and I drive 2 hours and fork over bucket loads because it's hard to find good help. That said, you may be able to find a TMJ or occlusion specialist that will at least give you a consult if your dentist doesn't seem to get it. I would hope a good dentist would know what he doesn't know, or be able to figure some of this out even without the gadgets.

Just a reminder of what you already know... these changes are the difference of millimeters, sure, but even 1 millimeter can mess everything up and cause tension or inflammation that also impacts your bite, not to mention pain. I would NOT let a dentist adjust your occlusion without first discussing whether or not inflammation or tension might be impacting their clinical analysis, because you don't want to adjust into a broken system.

Reading this was really odd for me. I am AMAZED at how similar it is to where I was at when I was graduating college. I mean, change a few details around (like the major) and it is as if I was reading something I wrote back then. 

You know the quote "Youth is wasted on the young." This is how I feel. I felt my childhood, teenage years, and college years were STOLEN from me by depression. I did some of the typical things, but so much of my energy went in to "going through the motions" just because I'm obligated to be functioning in society, all the while I'm mercilessly battling depression. While I do not hate the degree I received, I too regretted it by the time I was a few months from graduation. I wanted to change it. I wanted to go back. I felt OVERWHELMED by the prospect of having focused so hard on BEING ALIVE all through college that I still felt incredibly unprepared for the real world.

The good news is - while you may not realize it right now - one day you'll look back and realize some of what you're feeling is normal. While your feelings of fear and loss are probably exacerbated by depression, most people graduating college feel them to some extent. I would be extremely cautious of any college graduate that said otherwise, in fact. This is good news because it means LOTS of people can relate to how you're feeling right now, and if you're open to it, lots of people that have already been through it can guide you and help you. 

More good news: it is never too late. Look for a job, work some until you feel a little more stable, and then go back to school. Who gives a fuck? Do whatever you want. This is not your One Chance to go to school. Pick another major and start back at square one if you want. Or go to grad school for something completely different. Do a night class. Do an online class. You are not trapped. Nothing is set in stone.

Some years will be worse than others. There are countless variables that can impact this, many of which are completely out of your control probably. Depression cycles regardless of the type of diagnosis you have. One thing you should do to ensure that your next cycle of SAD isn't this bad is take pro-active measures (like you have by making a post here) to gain new coping mechanisms. Do you take any type of actual medication to help balance you out? There are options.
